newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian debt futures get fidgety over rates.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt futures get fidgety over rates.

text.p: Australian debt futures closed sharply higher as the market once again got fidgety over the domestic monetary policy outlook, brushing aside the post-budget disappointment that has overhung the market since Tuesday.
Bill futures were particularly perky, despite Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane reiterating his concern over recent wages growth in a speech in Melbourne.
However, he did say that the central bank would let the economy grow faster if it saw good news on wages and inflation, and would not panic about a short period of strong expansion.
In his testimony to a parliamentry finance committee last week Macfarlane said that he saw little economic gain from a cut in current 6.0 percent official interest rates.

"After listening to his semi-annual testimony and that speech at lunchtime he seems to be have fallen in love with 6.0 percent and he intends to maintain that love affair for as long as it takes," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
Bill futures kicked off with a bid tone as an influential U.S. bank was seen buying June futures, which traders said spooked the market going into Macfarlane's speech.
And even when Macfarlane said today that recent data on wages growth had been a setback to prospects for improving inflation, the bill strip advance continued.

Adding to the jittery conditions were misreported comments by Deputy Prime Minster Tim Fischer suggesting that another policy easing was on the way, when he actually told parliament that recent interest rate cuts had saved farmers A$300 million already with more savings to come.
June and September bill futures touched respective highs of 94.09 and 94.05 at one stage, equating to cash rate just below 6.0 Percent.

"I can see the reason why December and March (bill) contracts would have rallied, because there was a strong hint there that he (Macfarlane) might be willing to let the economy go and not hike rates early. But for the June, and even September, to go through cash was a little optimistic," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.

The market was also lifted by lessening concerns over a tightening by the Federal Reserve next Tuesday when the policy makers meet after the 0.6 percent fall in the April PPI reported on Wednesday. However, the U.S. market faces another raft of indicators later on Thursday which could swing sentiment again.
Local bond yields outperformed the dollar bloc across the curve, reclaiming lost ground since Tuesday night's budget.
U.S. Treasuries rallied on Wednesday on the PPI, but faces the April CPI, industrial production, capacity utilisation and the weekly jobless claims report later today.
